topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME** > - **Course:** PECST412 - PATTERN RECOGNITION > - **Module:** Module 4 > - **Topic:** Future Trends in Pattern Recognition # Section 1: Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview ## 1.1 Formal Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Terminology) > [!NOTE] > **Future Trends in Pattern Recognition** refer to the emerging paradigms, architectures, and computational methodologies that extend classical statistical and structural pattern recognition beyond hand-crafted features into **data-driven, self-supervised, generative, and interpretable** learning frameworks. They emphasize automation of feature extraction, scalability to unlabeled data, robustness to distribution shift, and integration with edge, federated, and neuromorphic computing substrates. In the KTU 2024 Scheme context, this module positions classical pattern recognition (Bayes, k-NN, SVM, HMM) as a *baseline* and surveys the modern continuum: | Era | Defining Paradigm | Limitation Driving "Future Trends" | |---|---|---| | 1960s–1990s | Statistical / Syntactic | Manual feature engineering | | 2000s | Kernel methods (SVM) | Poor scaling, no end-to-end learning | | 2012–2017 | Deep CNNs (AlexNet, ResNet) | Massive labelled data hunger | | 2017–2022 | Transformers, SSL, GANs | Opacity, centralization, energy cost | | 2023+ | Foundation models, XAI, Edge AI, Quantum-ML | Trust, privacy, deployment latency | ## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — Plain English Intuition > [!TIP] > **Analogy — The Evolving Doctor:** > - *Classical Pattern Recognition* is like a doctor who **only** uses a stethoscope and a checklist written 50 years ago. Accurate, but rigid. > - *Deep Learning* is the doctor who **learns** by looking at a million X-rays — brilliant, but cannot tell you *why* a diagnosis was made. > - *Future Trends* = the doctor who (a) learns from a million X-rays **without** anyone labeling them (**self-supervised learning**), (b) explains the diagnosis in plain English (**explainable AI**), (c) shares knowledge with other hospitals **without sharing patient data** (**federated learning**), and (d) runs a tiny diagnostic chip inside a wearable watch (**edge AI / TinyML**). This is the intellectual spine of Module 4. ## 1.3 The Seven Pillars of Future Trends (KTU High-Yield Classification) 1. **Deep Architectures beyond CNNs** — Vision Transformers (ViT), Swin, ConvNeXt. 2. **Self-Supervised Learning (SSL)** — SimCLR, MoCo, DINO, MAE. 3. **Generative Models** — VAE, GAN, Diffusion Models (DDPM, Stable Diffusion). 4. **Transfer & Few-Shot Learning** — Foundation models, prompt tuning, meta-learning (MAML). 5. **Federated & Privacy-Preserving Learning** — FedAvg, differential privacy, split learning. 6. **Explainable AI (XAI)** — Grad-CAM, SHAP, LIME, attention rollout. 7. **Edge / Neuromorphic / Quantum Pattern Recognition** — TinyML, spiking neural networks (SNN), QML kernels. ## 1.4 Physical & Empirical Constants Worth Memorizing > [!IMPORTANT] > - **ImageNet-1K benchmark Top-1 accuracy (2024 SOTA):** ≈ **91.1 %** (EVA-02 / ViT-G). > - **Standard ViT input patch size:** **16 × 16** pixels. > - **Contrastive temperature τ (SimCLR):** typically **0.07 – 0.5**. > - **Common diffusion steps (DDPM):** **1000** noising steps. > - **MobileNetV3 parameter budget (Edge AI):** ≈ **2.5 M parameters** for < 50 ms mobile inference. # Section 2: Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet ## 2.1 The "Why" Behind Each Future Trend ### 2.1.1 Why Self-Supervised Learning (SSL)? - **Problem:** Labelled data is expensive (medical imaging, satellite, rare-language NLP). - **How SSL solves it:** Create *pseudo-labels* from the data itself (e.g., predict the missing patch, predict rotation, contrast positive vs. negative pairs). - **Result:** Pre-train on **unlabelled** corpus, fine-tune on **tiny** labelled set → near-supervised accuracy. ### 2.1.2 Why Transformers over CNNs for Pattern Recognition? - CNNs have a **local receptive field** (limited inductive bias). Transformers use **self-attention** to relate *any* pair of tokens. - Self-attention is permutation-equivariant but with positional encodings, it models **long-range dependencies** critical in histopathology, remote sensing, and video. ### 2.1.3 Why Generative Models? - Pattern recognition traditionally = **discriminative** $P(y \vert x)$. - Future trend = **generative** $P(x)$ *and* $P(y \vert x)$. Generative models (VAE/GAN/Diffusion) model the full data distribution → enables anomaly detection, data augmentation, simulation. ### 2.1.4 Why Federated Learning? - GDPR / HIPAA / DPDP Act (India 2023) forbid raw-data sharing across hospitals / banks. - Federated learning trains one **global model** while data stays **on-device**. Only gradients are shared. ### 2.1.5 Why Explainable AI (XAI)? - EU AI Act 2024 mandates **transparency for high-risk systems** (medical, hiring, justice). - Black-box deep nets are not acceptable; XAI provides saliency maps, concept activation, and counterfactuals. ### 2.1.6 Why Edge / Neuromorphic Pattern Recognition? - Cloud round-trip latency = **50–200 ms** (unacceptable for autonomous driving at 30 Hz). - Edge inference on TinyML or SNN = **< 10 ms** with < 1 mW power. ### 2.1.7 Why Foundation Models + Few-Shot Learning? - Train one massive model on broad data → adapt to a *new* class with **1–5 examples** (1-shot, 5-shot). - Saves the cost of training a fresh network per task. --- ## 2.2 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet > [!NOTE] > The following table is the **exam-ready consolidated formula sheet** for Module 4 future-trends problems. All variables and units are KTU-standard. | # | Concept | Formula | Description / Units | |---|---|---|---| | 1 | Self-Attention | $\text{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\dfrac{Q K^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V$ | $Q, K, V \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_k}$; $\sqrt{d_k}$ = scaling factor for variance stability | | 2 | Multi-Head Attention | $\text{MHA}(Q,K,V) = [\text{head}_1;\dots;\text{head}_h]\,W^{O}$ | $h$ = number of heads; concatenation then linear projection | | 3 | Transformer Layer Norm | $y = \gamma \odot \dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma} + \beta$ | $\mu, \sigma$ over feature dim; $\gamma, \beta$ learnable | | 4 | NT-Xent (SimCLR) Contrastive Loss | $\ell_{i,j} = -\log \dfrac{\exp(\text{sim}(z_i,z_j)/\tau)}{\sum_{k=1}^{2N}\mathbb{1}_{[k\neq i]}\exp(\text{sim}(z_i,z_k)/\tau)}$ | $\tau$ = temperature (≈ 0.1); $\text{sim}$ = cosine similarity; positives = augmented pair | | 5 | InfoNCE Bound | $\mathcal{L}_{\text{NCE}} \geq -\mathbb{E}\!\left[\log \dfrac{\exp(s(x,c)/\tau)}{\sum_{\tilde{c}}\exp(s(x,\tilde{c})/\tau)}\right]$ | Lower bound on mutual information $I(x;c)$ | | 6 | VAE ELBO | $\log p(x) \geq \mathbb{E}_{q(z \vert x)}[\log p(x \vert z)] - D_{\text{KL}}\!\left(q(z \vert x)\,\Vert\,p(z)\right)$ | Reconstruction − KL regularizer | | 7 | GAN Objective (Min–Max) | $\min_{G}\max_{D}\, V(D,G) = \mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_{\text{data}}}[\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}_{z\sim p_z}[\log(1-D(G(z)))]$ | Two-player game | | 8 | Diffusion Forward Process | $q(x_t \vert x_{t-1}) = \mathcal{N}\!\left(x_t;\,\sqrt{1-\beta_t}\,x_{t-1},\,\beta_t I\right)$ | $\beta_t$ = noise schedule, $t \in [1,T]$, $T=1000$ | | 9 | Diffusion Closed Form | $x_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\,\epsilon,\quad \bar{\alpha}_t=\prod_{s=1}^{t}(1-\beta_s)$ | $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)$ | | 10 | DDPM Training Loss (Simplified) | $\mathcal{L}_{\text{simple}} = \mathbb{E}_{t,x_0,\epsilon}\!\left[\Vert \epsilon - \epsilon_{\theta}(x_t,t) \Vert^2\right]$ | Predict the noise | | 11 | FedAvg Update | $w_{t+1} = w_t - \eta \sum_{k=1}^{K}\dfrac{n_k}{n}\,\nabla \ell_k(w_t)$ | $n_k$ = samples on client $k$; $n=\sum n_k$ | | 12 | MAML Meta-Update | $\theta \leftarrow \theta - \alpha \nabla_{\theta}\sum_{\mathcal{T}_i\sim p(\mathcal{T})}\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{T}_i}\!\left(\theta - \alpha \nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{T}_i}(\theta)\right)$ | Inner + outer loop; $\alpha$ = inner LR | | 13 | Grad-CAM Saliency | $L^{c}_{\text{Grad-CAM}} = \text{ReLU}\!\left(\sum_{k} \alpha^{c}_{k}\, A^{k}\right),\ \ \alpha^{c}_{k} = \dfrac{1}{Z}\sum_{i,j}\dfrac{\partial Y^{c}}{\partial A^{k}_{ij}}$ | $A^k$ = $k$-th feature map; $Y^c$ = class score | | 14 | SHAP Value | $\phi_i = \sum_{S \subseteq F \setminus \{i\}}\dfrac{\vert S \vert !\,(\vert F \vert - \vert S \vert - 1)!}{\vert F \vert !}\,\big[f(S\cup\{i\}) - f(S)\big]$ | Additive feature attribution | | 15 | Spiking Neuron (LIF) | $\tau_m \dfrac{dv}{dt} = -(v - v_{\text{rest}}) + R\,I(t)$ | $v$ = membrane potential; $I(t)$ = input current; $\tau_m$ ≈ 10–20 ms | > [!WARNING] > **Markdown Table Hazard Avoided:** All set-builder / absolute-value notation uses `\vert` and `\Vert` instead of `|` so the markdown table parser never breaks. --- ## 2.3 Real-World Engineering Utility | Future Trend | Industry Use-Case | |---|---| | Vision Transformer (ViT) | Tumor segmentation in histopathology (CAMELYON16) | | Self-Supervised (DINOv2) | Defect detection with only 50 labelled images | | Diffusion Models | Synthetic data augmentation for rare-class fault detection in manufacturing | | Federated Learning | Multi-hospital COVID-19 CT classifier without sharing patient scans | | XAI (Grad-CAM) | Lawyer's evidence in court — *"why did the model reject this loan?"* | | TinyML / Edge AI | Keyword spotting on a ₹500 ESP32 wearable | | Quantum Kernel | High-dimensional feature maps for genomic pattern recognition | # Section 3: Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix > [!IMPORTANT] > Two landmark derivations follow. (A) The **self-attention mechanism** (foundation of ViT / Transformers). (B) The **NT-Xent contrastive loss** (foundation of self-supervised pattern recognition). Every algebraic step is shown in full. --- ## 3.1 Derivation A — Self-Attention as a Soft, Differentiable Retrieval ### 3.1.1 Setup Given an input sequence of $n$ tokens each of dimension $d$, project them into three matrices: - $Q = X W^{Q} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_k}$ - $K = X W^{K} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_k}$ - $V = X W^{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_v}$ where $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$ is the input embedding matrix, and $W^{Q}, W^{K}, W^{V}$ are learnable projection matrices. ### 3.1.2 Step-by-Step Derivation **Step 1 — Compute raw compatibility scores between every pair of tokens:** $$ S = Q K^{\top} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n} $$ Each entry $S_{ij} = q_i^{\top} k_j$ measures how much *query* token $i$ should attend to *key* token $j$. **Step 2 — Scale by $\sqrt{d_k}$ to keep gradients stable:** $$ \tilde{S}_{ij} = \dfrac{S_{ij}}{\sqrt{d_k}} $$ **Why?** If $q_i, k_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)$ with dimension $d_k$, then $\mathbb{E}[q_i^{\top} k_j]=0$ and $\mathrm{Var}(q_i^{\top} k_j)=d_k$. Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ gives unit variance, preventing the softmax from saturating. **Step 3 — Apply row-wise softmax to obtain attention weights (rows sum to 1):** $$ A_{ij} = \text{softmax}(\tilde{S})_{ij} = \dfrac{\exp(\tilde{S}_{ij})}{\sum_{j'=1}^{n} \exp(\tilde{S}_{ij'})} $$ Each row $A_i$ is now a probability distribution over the $n$ keys. **Step 4 — Aggregate values weighted by attention probabilities:** $$ \text{Attention}(Q,K,V) = A V \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_v} $$ **Step 5 — Compact final form (the canonical transformer equation):** $$ \text{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\dfrac{Q K^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V $$ This is the result that appears in every transformer paper. $\blacksquare$ --- ## 3.2 Derivation B — NT-Xent (Normalized Temperature-scaled Cross-Entropy) Loss for Self-Supervised Pattern Recognition This is the core loss function behind **SimCLR** (Chen et al., ICML 2020) — the canonical SSL framework for visual pattern recognition. ### 3.2.1 Setup - For each input image $x_i$ in a mini-batch of size $N$, generate **two random augmentations** $x_i, \tilde{x}_i$. - Encoder $f(\cdot)$ + projection head $g(\cdot)$ produce embeddings $z_i = g(f(x_i))$, $z_j = g(f(\tilde{x}_i)) \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$. - Cosine similarity: $\text{sim}(z_i, z_j) = z_i^{\top} z_j / (\Vert z_i\Vert \Vert z_j\Vert)$. - Effective batch size: $2N$. Each embedding has exactly **one positive** (its augmented twin) and $2N-2$ **negatives**. ### 3.2.2 Step-by-Step Derivation **Step 1 — Define the per-pair (positive pair $(i,j)$) loss:** $$ \ell_{i,j} = -\log \dfrac{\exp(\text{sim}(z_i, z_j)/\tau)}{\sum_{k=1}^{2N} \mathbb{1}_{[k \neq i]} \exp(\text{sim}(z_i, z_k)/\tau)} $$ The denominator implicitly excludes the anchor $i$ itself via the indicator $\mathbb{1}_{[k \neq i]}$. **Step 2 — Recognize this as a categorical cross-entropy over $2N-1$ classes:** The numerator is the score for the *true class* (positive pair); the denominator is the partition function summing scores for *all* other candidates. This is exactly the **softmax cross-entropy** form: $$ \ell_{i,j} = -\log \dfrac{\exp(s_{ij}/\tau)}{\sum_{k\neq i}\exp(s_{ik}/\tau)} $$ where $s_{ik} \equiv \text{sim}(z_i, z_k)$. **Step 3 — Symmetrize over both augmentation directions and average across the batch:** $$ \mathcal{L} = \dfrac{1}{2N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\big[\ell_{2i-1,\,2i} + \ell_{2i,\,2i-1}\big] $$ This symmetric form ensures that the positive pair $(i,j)$ contributes loss from both $i \to j$ and $j \to i$. **Step 4 — Information-theoretic interpretation (InfoNCE lower bound on mutual information):** Because the categorical cross-entropy is minimized when one class dominates, and the temperature $\tau$ controls the *peakiness* of the distribution, minimizing $\mathcal{L}$ is equivalent to **maximizing a lower bound on the mutual information** $I(z_i; z_j)$ between anchor and positive: $$ I(z_i; z_j) \geq \log(2N-1) - \mathcal{L} $$ **Why does this matter for pattern recognition?** Maximizing $I$ means the encoder $f(\cdot)$ preserves as much *task-relevant signal* as possible between an image and its augmented twin, while pushing apart unrelated images. The downstream classifier can then be a thin linear layer on top of these representations. $\blacksquare$ --- ## 3.3 Analytical Matrix — Choosing the Right Future Trend | Problem Characteristic | Recommended Future Trend | Justification | |---|---|---| | Few labels (< 100 per class) | Self-Supervised + Linear probe | Pre-train on abundant unlabelled data | | Long-range spatial / temporal dependencies | Transformer (ViT / Swin / TimeSformer) | Global receptive field via attention | | Need to generate new samples (e.g., data aug) | Diffusion model | State-of-the-art FID scores 2023+ | | Privacy-bound multi-institution data | Federated Learning | Data never leaves the institution | | Regulated / high-stakes decision | XAI wrapper (Grad-CAM + SHAP) | Provides human-verifiable explanation | | Battery-powered, sub-100 ms inference | TinyML / SNN | < 1 mW, on-device | | Many related tasks, one task per client | Foundation model + prompt / LoRA tuning | Reuse weights; tiny parameter update | | Quantum-available hardware | Quantum kernel SVM | Exponential feature-space advantage | # Section 4: Structural Diagrams & Schematics > [!NOTE] > Two Mermaid block diagrams are provided. How does it differ from supervised and unsupervised learning in the context of pattern recognition?** **Model Answer (3 marks):** - **Definition (1 mark):** Self-supervised learning (SSL) is a learning paradigm in which the supervisory signal is **automatically generated from the input data itself** (e.g., predicting a masked patch, predicting rotation angle, or contrasting augmented pairs), eliminating the need for human-annotated labels. - **vs. Supervised (1 mark):** Supervised learning requires **manually labelled** $(x, y)$ pairs; SSL creates *pseudo-labels* from the data structure, hence needs **no human annotation**. - **vs. Unsupervised (1 mark):** Pure unsupervised methods (e.g., k-means, PCA) discover structure *without* any target; SSL still optimizes a *defined objective* (predict a known transformation) and is therefore positioned between supervised and unsupervised learning. ### Q2. `[KTU University Exam - Dec 2023]` **List any three future trends in pattern recognition and state one real-world application of each.** **Model Answer (3 marks):** 1. **Vision Transformers (ViT)** — used in **medical tumor segmentation** from histopathology slides. 2. **Federated Learning** — used in **multi-hospital COVID-19 CT classification** without sharing patient scans. 3. **Explainable AI (XAI)** — used in **loan-approval systems** to provide legally defensible reasons for rejections (Grad-CAM / SHAP). *(Alternative accepted: Diffusion models, TinyML, Graph Neural Networks, Neuromorphic computing.)* --- ## Part B — 14-Mark Questions (Module Internal Choice) > [!IMPORTANT] > Two fully independent 14-mark questions are given. ViT Architecture (3 marks):** The Vision Transformer treats an image $X \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C}$ as a sequence of patches. Steps: 1. **Patchify:** Split image into $n = (H \cdot W) / P^2$ non-overlapping patches of size $P \times P$ (typically $P=16$). 2. **Linear Embedding:** Project each patch to a $D$-dim vector via a learnable matrix $E$. 3. **Position Encoding:** Add learnable 1-D positional embeddings $E_{\text{pos}} \in \mathbb{R}^{(n+1) \times D}$ to retain spatial information (transformers are permutation-equivariant without this). 4. **CLS Token:** Prepend a learnable $z_0$ token; its final-layer representation is used for classification. 5. **Transformer Encoder:** $L$ stacked blocks, each containing **Multi-Head Self-Attention (MSA)** + **LayerNorm** + **MLP** with residual connections. 6. **MLP Head:** A linear classifier on the final `[CLS]` token. **2. Self-Attention Derivation (3 marks):** (See Section 3.1 derivation — write Step 1 to Step 5 of the compact attention formula.) **3. ViT vs CNN for Long-Range Patterns (1 mark):** - CNN kernels are **local**; deeper layers enlarge the receptive field only through stacking. - ViT's self-attention connects **any two patches in $O(1)$ layers**, modelling long-range dependencies (e.g., tumor cells in opposite corners of a pathology slide). --- #### Model Solution — Q.A (b) **1. Empirically this linear probe reaches > 90 % of the supervised accuracy using only **1 % of the labels**, demonstrating the value of SSL for low-label pattern recognition. --- ### ❑ Question B — 14 Marks `[KTU University Exam - Model Paper 2024]` **(a) What are Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)? Derive the min-max objective and explain the training dynamics. Compare GANs with Diffusion Models for image-pattern synthesis.** **(7 marks)** **(b) Explain Federated Learning for privacy-preserving pattern recognition. Derive the FedAvg aggregation rule and discuss its advantages and key challenges.** **(7 marks)** --- #### Model Solution — Q.B (a) **1. GAN Definition & Architecture (2 marks):** A GAN (Goodfellow et al., 2014) consists of two networks trained in opposition: - **Generator $G$:** maps noise $z \sim p_z$ to a fake sample $G(z)$ that mimics real data. - **Discriminator $D$:** outputs the probability that an input is real. **2. Min-Max Objective Derivation (3 marks):** The discriminator tries to assign probability **1** to real samples and **0** to fakes. Its cross-entropy objective is: $$ \max_{D}\, V(D) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}}[\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z}[\log(1 - D(G(z)))] $$ The generator wants to *fool* $D$ by maximizing the second term (i.e., $D(G(z)) \to 1$). This leads to the two-player game: $$ \min_{G} \max_{D}\, V(D,G) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}}[\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z}[\log(1 - D(G(z)))] $$ At the Nash equilibrium, $p_G = p_{\text{data}}$ and $D(x) = \tfrac{1}{2}$ everywhere — $D$ cannot distinguish real from fake. **3. GAN vs Diffusion Models (2 marks):** | Aspect | GAN | Diffusion Model | |---|---|---| | Training stability | Mode collapse, unstable | Stable, well-defined ELBO | | Sample quality (FID) | Excellent (StyleGAN) | SOTA (Stable Diffusion, DALL·E 3) | | Sampling speed | Single forward pass — **fast** | 20–1000 denoising steps — **slow** | | Likelihood estimation | Not tractable | Tractable lower bound | | Conditional control | Difficult | Excellent (classifier-free guidance) | **Conclusion:** Diffusion models dominate 2024-era *high-quality synthesis*; GANs remain useful for *real-time generation*. --- #### Model Solution — Q.B (b) **1. Federated Learning Definition (2 marks):** Federated Learning (FL), introduced by McMahan et al. (2017), is a decentralized training paradigm where **multiple clients** (hospitals, phones, banks) collaboratively train a **single global model** under the coordination of a central server, **without exposing their local raw data**. **2. FedAvg Aggregation Derivation (3 marks):** Let $K$ clients each hold $n_k$ samples with $n = \sum_k n_k$. Each client computes a local gradient $g_k = \nabla \ell_k(w_t)$ on its data. The server's goal is to approximate the centralized gradient: $$ g_{\text{cent}} = \nabla\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K} \dfrac{n_k}{n}\,\ell_k\right) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \dfrac{n_k}{n}\,\nabla \ell_k(w_t) $$ Hence, the FedAvg update is: $$ w_{t+1} = w_t - \eta \sum_{k=1}^{K} \dfrac{n_k}{n}\, g_k $$ Equivalently, after $E$ local SGD epochs each client pushes $w_k$ to the server, which averages them: $$ w_{t+1} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \dfrac{n_k}{n}\, w_k $$ **3. Advantages and Challenges (2 marks):** | Advantages | Challenges | |---|---| | **Privacy preservation** — raw data never leaves the device | **Heterogeneity** (non-IID data across clients) | | **Reduced communication** vs. centralized | **Stragglers** (slow clients delay rounds) | | **Regulatory compliance** (GDPR, HIPAA, DPDP) | **Gradient leakage** attacks (mitigated by differential privacy) | | **Edge personalization** possible | **Convergence drift** under skewed data | --- > [!WARNING] > **KTU Examiner's Valuation Warning — Common Pitfalls** > 1. **Do NOT skip the derivation steps** in 14-mark sub-parts; the formula alone is worth at most **1 mark**.
